commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Require cudnn-frontend >=1.31.0: cuDNN could replay an unloaded kernel from a CUDA graph
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Raise the `nvidia-cudnn-frontend` floor in `requirements/cuda.txt` from
`1.19.1` to `1.31.0`, the first release containing
[NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend#1195](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/pull/1195),
"Keep execution plans alive for the CUDA graphs recorded from them".

Before that fix, cuDNN could unload a just-in-time compiled kernel's library
when the last cuDNN owner of it went away, while a CUDA graph still contained
a node that launched that kernel. Replaying the graph then dispatched whatever
had taken over that code address. The upstream fix makes the graph hold a
reference for as long as it can launch the kernel.

The affected `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0-ubuntu2404` stack has both conditions:

- `FlashInferFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel` is first in `_POSSIBLE_FP8_KERNELS` for
  CUDA and calls `bmm_fp8(..., backend="auto")`. Because
  `requirements/cuda.txt` declares `nvidia-cudnn-frontend`, the `cudnn` module
  is importable and `auto` admits the cuDNN runner.
- FlashInfer memoises those cuDNN graphs in
  `functools.lru_cache(maxsize=2048)`, keyed per shape, and the cache evicts
  cold entries. The GEMMs themselves are captured into the decode CUDA graphs.

In that stack, an eviction can release the last owner of a kernel that a live decode graph
still launches. The observable outcomes are an illegal-address fault, a CUDA
error reported at synchronisation, or — the case that matters most for a
serving stack — **silently wrong output with no error reported at all**.

FlashInfer 0.7.2, pinned by the tested base, now has a
[capture-retention helper](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.2/flashinfer/gemm/gemm_base.py#L3761-L3774)
that keeps captured cuDNN GEMM graphs alive for the process lifetime. This
separately mitigates the GEMM eviction path on current `main`. The frontend
floor still ensures that cudnn-frontend's own CUDA-graph lifetime fix is
installed.

## What this fixes

| Issue | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| #52225 | root cause identified directly | The investigation that led here, and the attribution is not statistical. A GPU coredump and CUDA-GDB independently confirmed the faulting kernel as `cudnn_generated_fort_native_sm80_matMul_pointwise_pointwise_knob_0_256x128x128_3_0`, launched with block (384,1,1) against a cubin declaring a 256-thread launch bound and 246 registers — the instruction-issue rejection that reports as Xid 13 `Out Of Range Register`. In the retained fault run, the cuDNN LRU eviction destroying a cold captured graph's plans and runtime kernels was observed directly, 436 µs after a newly compiled graph of a different shape, with the evicted kernel's CUDA graph node still live and no host launch since its capture 66 minutes earlier. A source audit confirmed no graph retention existed in the deployed cuDNN. That is the mechanism this fix removes. |
| #55571 | likely fixed | A third-party report, so the attribution is indirect: no coredump of their fault was analysed and no run on their hardware used the fixed wheel. What makes it strong is that *either* `VLLM_DISABLED_KERNELS=FlashInferFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel` *or* `--enforce-eager` reportedly makes it go away, and those remove exactly the two conditions this defect needs — the cuDNN lane, and CUDA graph capture. |

Deliberately **not** claimed:

- **#61007** (GB10 hang inside a cuDNN FP8 GEMM) is the same lane but a
  different failure: an unbounded host-side hang while cuDNN builds a plan
  lazily per shape in the hot path. This change does not address plan
  construction cost. #57209 is the change aimed at that.
- **#61069, #60119, #59768, #49926** share the Xid 13 or illegal-access
  symptom class but implicate other kernel families, and in #60119's case the
  report itself declines to claim a common root cause. No evidence either way.

## Relationship to #57209

[#57209](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57209) pins `bmm_fp8` to
cuBLAS on sm_12x, avoiding the cuDNN lane. This PR fixes the lane instead, by
taking the upstream fix, and is not an alternative proposal to it: #57209 also
cites host-side plan-construction latency in the serving hot path, which a
frontend bump does not change. If #57209 lands, this bump still matters for
every other cuDNN consumer reached through cudnn-frontend — the
`flashinfer_cudnn` NVFP4 linear backend and the cuDNN ViT and multimodal
encoder attention paths — and for sm_100 and sm_121, which #57209 does not
cover.

## Why the frontend and not the backend

Both upstream fixes work and each is sufficient alone: cuDNN 9.27.0.42 fixes it
for every caller including torch's own, while the frontend fix covers
cudnn-frontend consumers only.

In fairness to upstream, they consider the backend the thorough fix and the
frontend a workaround, and the frontend fix retains the whole `ExecutionPlan`
where the backend retains only the kernel code — so it holds more memory per
plan captured into a live graph. That cost is not quantified here.

The frontend is still the right change *for vLLM*: vLLM already declares a
floor for it and this is one line, whereas pinning `nvidia-cudnn-cu13` would
override the cuDNN version torch resolves transitively. Upstream chose to
write the frontend fix for exactly this reason — so that frameworks could pick
it up without waiting on a backend upgrade — and it is the vehicle they
offered for this report.

The consequence is stated plainly: cuDNN callers that do not go through
cudnn-frontend are unaffected by this PR. In vLLM that means torch
convolutions (`vllm/model_executor/layers/conv.py`) and torch's
`SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION` (`phi4mm_utils.py`). Those are fixed when torch's
transitive cuDNN pin reaches 9.27.0.42, which is the right lever for them; they
are not known to be affected today. If maintainers would rather take the
thorough fix, the backend pin is the alternative and I am happy to switch —
but it should be one or the other, since applying both creates two user
objects for the same kernel.

Upstream has already commented on #52225 pointing at the frontend fix:
<https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52225#issuecomment-5900569717>.

## Test plan and results

Hardware: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (sm_120), driver 580.126.20.

**Frontend fix, either side of the upstream merge commit**, with the backend
wheel as a second axis — 96 cells each side across backends 9.19.0.56 through
9.26.0.51, varying graph construction, workload profile, kernel-cache size and
owner-lifetime arm:

| frontend | reproducing cells |
|---|---|
| `07c939a6cce4` (pre-fix) | 22 of 96 |
| `4d4e428bd747` (PR #1195) | **0 of 96** |

Every reproducing cell is in the arm that releases the owner. The paired
`retain` and `user-object` arms are clean on both sides, which is what makes
this a comparison rather than an absence of failure.

**Backend fix on the public wheel**, with the pre-fix frontend held fixed so
the wheel is the only variable, run control-first within each configuration:

| configuration | 9.20.0.48 | 9.27.0.42 |
|---|---|---|
| populate, cache default/off, release | `SIGSEGV` | clean |
| stream capture, cache default/off, release | CUDA error 718, invalid program counter | clean |
| profile 52225, cache default/off, release | **3,948,544 of 5,275,648 elements wrong, 2,637,824 non-finite, `sync_status=0`** | clean, 0 mismatches |
| all six of the above, retain arm | clean | clean |

The wrong-result rows report no error to the host. The 9.27.0.42 release notes
carry the matching entry: "Runtime-compiled kernel code now stays loaded for
as long as a CUDA graph can launch it."

**The fix is in the binary vLLM actually imports.** vLLM reaches cuDNN through
FlashInfer's `import cudnn`, the compiled module in the wheel, not through
headers:

| wheel | `cuda_graph_retention.h` | retention symbols in `_compiled_module*.so` |
|---|---|---|
| 1.30.0 | absent | 0 |
| 1.31.0 | present | 41 |

**Cost**, measured on the stock `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0-ubuntu2404` image
with only the frontend wheel swapped, three repetitions per arm, medians:

| measurement | 1.28.0 | 1.31.0 |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA graph replay | 45.04 µs | 45.04 µs |
| CUDA graph capture | 192.0 µs | 229.1 µs |
| plan build | 7655 µs | 7710 µs |
| max relative error vs cuBLAS | 0.000000 | 0.000000 |

Replay is unchanged, so the steady-state decode path pays nothing. Capture
costs about 37 µs more, once per captured graph at warmup, and the capture
ranges do not overlap across repetitions. The plan-build difference is within
noise at three samples. Numerics are unchanged against the cuBLAS backend.

Eager execution, measured separately because the cost might not be specific to
graphs — per-call host time with GPU work left asynchronous, two repetitions of
seven rounds — shows no regression either: 1.31.0 medians 95.80 and 94.88 µs
against 1.28.0's noisier 112.10 and 95.34 µs, with overlapping ranges.

One nuance for anyone assessing exposure: from backend 9.22 onward the pre-fix
frontend stops reproducing at the default kernel-cache size and still
reproduces with the cache disabled, because the cache was holding a second
reference. Backend version alone therefore does not tell you whether a
deployment is exposed.

Note also that `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0` resolves cudnn-frontend **1.28.0**
against the declared floor of 1.19.1, so the effective bump for that image is
1.28.0 → 1.31.0.

## Not measured

- **No end-to-end serving before-and-after with the released wheel.** The
  mechanism is directly established and the fix is verified on the
  deterministic reproducer, but the remaining step — serving the affected
  model at full exposure on the released wheel and showing the fault rate go
  to zero — is a multi-hour stochastic measurement and is not included. An
  earlier run with both fixes built from source did not reproduce the bug on
  Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4.
- **Read the lane ablation carefully if you cite it.** Disabling the
  FlashInfer FP8 class gave 7 of 12 against 0 of 12 at p≈0.0023 on the
  *family* endpoint (any `0x0d`/`0x0e`/`0x0f` fault in a cuDNN matMul); on the
  exact `0x0d` subtype alone it is 1 of 12 against 0 of 12, p=0.5 and
  uninformative. It corroborates that the lane is necessary; it is not the
  basis for the root-cause attribution, which is the coredump evidence above.
- **A Python-level reproduction was attempted and failed to fault its own
  control**, so it proves nothing in either direction and is not offered as
  evidence. The deterministic reproducer pins the engine and kernel config for
  both the target and the reoccupying donor, and FlashInfer's Python API
  exposes no way to select either.
- **The memory retained by the frontend fix is not quantified.** It keeps the
  whole execution plan alive per plan captured into a live graph, where the
  backend fix keeps only the kernel code.
- **No specific models are claimed as fixed.** There are internal reports that
  the backend upgrade resolved corruption for some FP8 Nemotron checkpoints,
  but they are soak observations without a paired control, so they are not
  offered here as evidence.
- The plan-build cost difference and cuDNN 9.28's expected opt-out are
  unresolved here.

## Duplicate check

- `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "cudnn-frontend in:body OR cudnn frontend in:title"` — no open PR changes this floor.
- `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "52225 in:body"` — one unrelated MoE PR.
- #57209 is the nearest open work; it avoids the lane rather than fixing it, and the difference is described above.

## AI assistance

This change was prepared with AI assistance. Every line of the diff and every
number above was reviewed by the submitter, the measurements were run on
first-party hardware, and the cells that were not measured are labelled as
such rather than inferred.

commits.pr_title: [KV Connector] Support sleep mode with the NIXL pull connector
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Stacked on #59625; only the last commit is new. This replaces the earlier lease-based revision of this PR (and the
closed #59713): there is no lease and no new protocol between engines.

#59625 refuses sleep mode with NIXL because peers keep the stale KV cache registration. Sleep keeps the virtual
addresses and maps new physical pages, so everything NIXL bound to the old pages goes stale: the memory registration
(rkeys), the local prepped dlists, the handshake payload served to peers, and each peer's loaded remote agent.

Evidence on #59625 with the NIXL refusal forced off (GB300, cross-node 1P1D, Qwen3-8B, UCX RDMA over RoCE):

- After a decode sleep and wake: 0/30 outputs match the awake control. After a prefill sleep and wake: 0/30.
- No errors and no failed transfers: on GB300 there is no `nvidia_peermem`, so UCX registers GPU memory through
  dmabuf, and the stale MR pins the old pages; peers read old data without any error.
- Sleep frees nothing of the KV cache (67763 MiB asleep instead of 2077), and after the wake the GPU holds both
  (150787 MiB instead of 85101).

This PR implements the #59625 hooks for the NIXL pull connector (`NixlConnector` / `NixlPullConnector`):

- `release_kv_caches()` (before the unmap): waits until no own read is in flight and no handshake is pending (bounded,
  `TimeoutError` keeps the registration), then releases every local prepped dlist, drops every remote engine (their
  split handles reference local memory; they are re-handshaked on demand), and deregisters the KV cache.
- `restore_kv_caches()` (after the remap): registers the same descriptors again, re-preps the local dlist, and
  rebuilds the handshake payload with the new agent metadata.
- Peer refresh through the existing handshake only:
  - After a wake-up that restored the KV cache (`tags` is None or contains `kv_cache`), `EngineCore` hands the
    workers' payloads to the scheduler (the startup code, extracted).
  - The scheduler-side connector owns the registration epoch: each republish bumps it and stamps the same epoch on
    every rank's payload, so ranks cannot advertise different epochs, even after a partly failed release.
  - The side-channel listener serves the new payloads; `request_finished` adds `remote_registration_epoch` to
    `kv_transfer_params`.
  - The reader records the epoch of the payloads it loaded (the minimum over the remote ranks of one handshake, in
    case it straddled the republish). A request naming a newer epoch drops that remote engine and handshakes again
    through the existing path; while reads through the old registration are still in flight, the request is
    re-queued instead. Older epochs never trigger a re-handshake.
  - The reader checks whether the agent is loaded once per request (`_start_read`), so a handshake that completes
    concurrently cannot install an old agent between the epoch check and the read.
- Under sleep mode the worker sets `UCX_RCACHE_ENABLE=n` and `UCX_TLS=^cuda_ipc` right before creating the agent,
  each only if the user did not set it, and logs once which defaults it applied (as `UCX_RCACHE_MAX_UNRELEASED` in
  `nixl_utils.py` does). **They are process-wide**: other UCX users in the worker process (the NIXL EPLB communicator,
  the EC NIXL connector, NVSHMEM with a UCX transport) and child processes inherit them.
  - UCX's registration cache defers the real deregistration. On GB300 the cached dmabuf MR kept the released pages
    pinned in about half of the sleeps, and `release_kv_cache_memory` freed nothing. With the cache off, every sleep
    freed the KV cache.
  - A peer's cuda_ipc import (intra-node NVLink or MNNVL) pins the exporter's pages inside the peer's UCX cache. Over
    MNNVL the outputs stayed correct, but the prefiller's KV cache stayed resident asleep and was doubled after the
    wake. Without cuda_ipc in the exporter's UCX context no peer can import it; reads use RDMA (on one node: RDMA
    loopback through the NIC). Cost measured below: none on GB300.
- Static policy, checked once at startup: `NixlPullConnector.supports_sleep_mode` is True only with the UCX backend
  (`backends == ["UCX"]`), the only one validated. `NixlPushConnector` stays refused: the producer writes through the
  decoder's registration and is not refreshed.
- `NIXL_CONNECTOR_VERSION` 13 -> 14 (payload field and `kv_transfer_params` key). Routers must forward
  `kv_transfer_params` unchanged, as they already must for `remote_block_ids`.

## Test Plan

- Unit tests (CPU-capable, fake NIXL agent), organized around invariants:
  - `test_decoder_reads_from_republished_prefiller[all-ranks|one-rank|straddled]` (scheduler level, real side
    channel): whichever ranks re-registered, a handshake after the republish loads the epoch the prefiller
    advertises, so the decoder reads instead of handshaking again; a handshake that straddled the republish is redone
    exactly once. The `one-rank` row (one rank's restore was a no-op) livelocks on the previous revision of this PR.
  - `test_sleep_cycle_releases_and_restores_registration`: with a tracking agent, nothing built on the registration
    survives a release (registrations, local and remote dlists, remote agents), and a restore registers the same memory
    with exactly one local dlist and publishes the new agent metadata; both calls idempotent over two cycles.
  - `test_release_waits_for_reads_and_handshakes`: an in-flight read or a pending handshake holds the release; a wedged
    one times out and keeps the registration; shutdown while released does not deregister again.
  - `TestPeerReplacement::test_rehandshakes_re_registered_peer`: same epoch reads through the loaded agent; a newer
    epoch drops it and handshakes again; with reads in flight the request is deferred until they finish.
  - `test_sleep_mode_ucx_defaults`: the UCX defaults under sleep mode only, and a user setting wins per variable.
  - `test_config.py`: NIXL pull supported, NIXL with a non-UCX backend and NIXL push refused, MultiConnector rows.
  - `test_engine_core.py::test_wake_up_republishes_kv_connector_handshake_metadata[all|kv_cache|weights]`: republish
    after the executor woke up, and only when the KV cache was restored.
- Mutation check: every piece of the change altered on its own, including the previous revision's worker-owned epoch.
- `pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/{test_nixl_connector,test_config,test_mooncake_connector,test_multi_connector}.py
  tests/v1/engine/test_engine_core.py tests/v1/worker/test_sleep_mode_backend.py`; the NIXL and config files 5 times;
  pre-commit on the changed files.
- Hardware: NVIDIA GB300 Slurm cluster, NUMA-local to the only active NIC (mlx5_4, RoCE, GID 3). Image: vLLM nightly
  aarch64 + this branch as per-file mounts with sha256 gates (all 12 mounted files equal to this commit). NIXL 1.4.1
  (bundled UCX). Qwen3-8B, prefix caching off, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.3`, level-1 sleep, UCX settings left to
  the branch defaults. Toy proxy from `tests/v1/kv_connector/nixl_integration`. Each check sends 30 prompts of
  1.1k-1.7k tokens (greedy, 32 tokens) and compares them with the awake control; transfers are counted from NIXL's KV
  transfer metrics and the logs are scanned for transfer failures and UCX errors. The UCX protocol in use is taken
  from `UCX_PROTO_INFO=y`.
  - Cross-node: P and D on two nodes, one GPU each.
  - Single node: P on GPUs 0-1 and D on GPUs 2-3 (TP2 each), with and without sleep mode, plus a transfer benchmark
    (30 sequential requests of ~1.3k and ~5k tokens, twice; 128 requests at concurrency 32), with transfer time and
    bytes from D's `vllm:nixl_xfer_time_seconds` and `vllm:nixl_bytes_transferred`.

## Test Result

Cross-node 1P1D TP1 (final commit; UCX picked `rc_mlx5` zero-copy GPU-to-GPU reads). "Asleep" and "woken" are MiB on
the slept GPU; awake is 85101 MiB.

| Case | Cycles | After every wake | Asleep | Woken | Failed transfers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sleep D | 3 | 30/30 | 2077 | 85101 | 0 |
| Sleep P | 3 | 30/30 | 2077 | 85101 | 0 |
| Sleep both | 3 | 30/30 | 2077 / 2077 | 85101 | 0 |
| Selective wake, weights then kv_cache (both) | 1 | 30/30 | 2077 -> 19415 -> 85101 | | 0 |
| Selective wake, kv_cache then weights (both) | 1 | 30/30 | 2077 -> 68809 -> 85101 | | 0 |
| `release_kv_cache_memory` on both (pause wait, release, wake kv_cache, resume) | 1 | 30/30 | P 20983, D 19415 | 85101 | 0 |
| P sleep (mode=wait) under load: 90 requests at concurrency 30, wake after 5 s | 1 | 0 errors; 30/30 after | 2077 | 85101 | 0 |

- The decoder re-handshakes exactly once per wake that restored the KV cache, including the selective wakes (the
  weights-only step no longer republishes); the first request after a wake takes 0.21-0.24 s versus 0.18 s.
- Under load, 18/90 outputs differ from the sequential control, as in a concurrent run without any sleep (batching
  noise); every post-wake check is 30/30.

Single node, P on GPUs 0-1, D on GPUs 2-3, TP2 each (sleep mode with the branch defaults, so reads use RDMA loopback):

| Case | Cycles | After every wake | Asleep (2 GPUs) | Woken | Failed transfers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sleep D / P / both | 3 each | 30/30 | 7166 | 172934 | 0 |
| `release_kv_cache_memory` on both | 1 | 30/30 | P 26054, D 25194 | 172934 | 0 |

Single-node transfer cost of the `UCX_TLS=^cuda_ipc` default (medians of two launches each; "transfer" is NIXL's
per-transfer time, one transfer per TP rank and request):

| Workload | Without sleep mode: cuda_ipc (NVLink) | Sleep mode: RDMA loopback | Without sleep mode, `UCX_TLS=^cuda_ipc` |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~1.3k tokens, sequential: request p50 | 59 ms | 54 ms | 52 ms |
| ~1.3k tokens: transfer time / rate (90 MB) | 8.0-8.9 ms / 10-11 GB/s | 4.0-4.6 ms / 20-22 GB/s | 4.1 ms / 22 GB/s |
| ~5k tokens, sequential: request p50 | 101-119 ms | 85 ms | 84 ms |
| ~5k tokens: transfer time / rate (355 MB) | 28-36 ms / 10-13 GB/s | 15.1 ms / 23.5 GB/s | 15.0 ms / 23.7 GB/s |
| 128 requests at concurrency 32, ~1.3k / ~5k tokens | 91-96 / 30.8 req/s | 117.5 / 32.8 req/s | 120.7 / 32.4 req/s |

- **No NVLink cost was measured on GB300**: with UCX's defaults, RDMA loopback through the NIC was faster than
  cuda_ipc for these transfers (cuda_ipc spent 5-29 ms per transfer in posting). This is UCX 1.4.1-bundled cuda_ipc
  between two instances with disjoint `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`; a tuned cuda_ipc setup, or a node whose NIC is slower
  relative to NVLink, may differ. Users who want cuda_ipc can set `UCX_TLS` themselves; then a peer's import keeps the
  slept KV cache resident (measured over MNNVL: 67763 MiB asleep, 150787 MiB after the wake; `UCX_CUDA_IPC_CACHE=n` on
  the reader frees it at +140 ms per request).
- Baseline (#59625 head with the refusal forced off) under the cross-node harness: decode sleep 0/30, prefill sleep
  0/30, 0 errors, KV cache pinned asleep (67763 MiB) and doubled after the wake (150787 MiB).
- Earlier revision of this PR at scale (same peer-refresh path): V4-Flash TP4+TP4 cross-node 30/30 cycles, 900/900
  probes, 23,792 transfers, 0 failed; Qwen3-8B 100/100 cycles, 0 failed.
- Unit: 391 passed across the files above. The failures are tests that need models this node cannot download (gated
  `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct`, and `test_engine_core_tp`, `_concurrent_batches` and
  `_invalid_request_id_type`); run alone on #59625's head, the same 4 fail. The NIXL and config files: 5 repeats,
  208 passed each time. Mutation check: 37 mutants, all killed; every
  new test kills at least one. The reviewer's fix probes pass (28/28).

Known limitations:
- **Host memory grows by about 1.3 MiB per sleep cycle on both P and D** (measured on the previous revision with
  `smaps_rollup` Rss at Qwen3-8B TP1, `num_threads=4`: 1.25-1.34 MiB/cycle, linear over 500 cycles; Mooncake and sleep
  without a connector are flat). Each re-handshake creates and closes UCX RC endpoints, and UCX does not return their
  send-queue buffers (about 640 KiB pinned per side per re-handshake, plus allocator fragmentation). The cost scales
  with NIXL threads and TP ranks (`num_threads=1` cuts it to 2/5). This revision keeps exactly one re-handshake per
  wake. Follow-up: keep the remote agent across a wake and reload only the peer's memory sections (NIXL partial
  metadata without connection info), which needs NIXL to replace the old sections of a loaded agent; that is not
  verified for NIXL 1.4.1. The UCX endpoint leak itself is to be reported upstream.
- NIXL backends other than UCX (refused), push mode (refused), and cuda_ipc/MNNVL transfers under sleep mode (disabled
  by default; a user who sets `UCX_TLS` with cuda_ipc keeps the peers' imports pinned, as measured above).
- A release that fails on one TP rank (timeout or deregistration error) leaves that worker released while
  `Executor.sleep` reports the engine awake, so nothing restores it. Partial-failure handling belongs to the executor
  and is shared with #59625's other connectors; it is not changed here. The registration epoch no longer diverges
  across ranks in that case, because the scheduler stamps it.
- With `enforce_handshake_compat: false`, a version-13 decoder ignores the epoch and never refreshes after a
  version-14 prefiller wakes; with the rcache-off default that shows up as failed transfers.

---

commits.pr_title: [Model] Support hotwords for MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

`MossTranscribeDiarizeForConditionalGeneration.get_generation_prompt` ignores `stt_params.hotwords`, so `hotwords` sent to `/v1/audio/transcriptions` is silently dropped for MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize (only Fun-ASR consumes it today). This PR appends the hotwords to the prompt using the [model card's hotword recipe](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize) (`<instruction>热词提示：w1, w2`).

Not a duplicate: no open PR or issue touches MOSS hotwords (`gh pr list --state open --search "hotwords"` / `"MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize"`). #50362 (verbose_json) edits the same model file in a different function and does not conflict.

## Claims

- `hotwords` now takes effect for MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize, with or without a custom `prompt`. Blank `hotwords` keeps the old prompt byte-for-byte.
- With a short relevant list, error rates on hotwords roughly halve on public biasing benchmarks (tables below); overall WER/CER also drops.
- Documents `hotwords` (previously undocumented) in the speech-to-text guide, including a note that long or unrelated lists can hurt accuracy.

## Validation

Setup: RTX 6000 Ada, nightly wheel at the base commit plus this patch, `vllm serve OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize --trust-remote-code`, `temperature=0`.

**Unit tests**: `pytest tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_moss_transcribe_diarize.py`: before the patch 2 failed (`hotwords`, `custom-prompt-hotwords`); after, 14 passed.

**E2E reproducer**: `curl localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions -F model=moss -F file=@clip.wav -F temperature=0 -F hotwords="珞珈数科, 钛动科技"`. Before the patch the output was identical to sending no hotwords; after, it is identical to writing the model card recipe into `prompt` by hand (洛嘉数科 -> 珞珈数科). Outputs without hotwords are unchanged.

**Public biasing benchmarks** (real speech, short relevant lists):

| benchmark | metric | no hotwords | `hotwords` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aishell1-NE, 808 utts | CER / hard-hotword recall | 6.46% / 18.3% | **2.54% / 93.8%** |
| LibriSpeech test-clean, N=100 | WER / B-WER | 2.23% / 9.45% | **2.02% / 5.05%** |
| LibriSpeech test-other, N=100 | WER / B-WER | 4.93% / 21.54% | **3.83% / 10.39%** |

<details>
<summary>Full tables (distractors, long lists, English recipe)</summary>

Aishell1-NE (from [SeACo-Paraformer](https://github.com/R1ckShi/SeACo-Paraformer); R1 = hard hotwords):

| hotwords | CER | hotword recall | R1 recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | 6.46% | 58.7% | 18.3% |
| hotwords in the utterance | 2.54% | 96.8% | 93.8% |
| + 20 distractors | 3.18% | 92.3% | 84.3% |
| full 400-word list | 9.83%* | 72.2% | 49.2% |

\* Excludes 8 runaway utterances; 95.33% with them.

LibriSpeech rare-word biasing ([Le et al. 2021](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fbai-speech/tree/master/is21_deep_bias), official `score.py`), scored on utterances where no condition ran away (output > 2x reference + 5 words): 2465/2620 test-clean, 2770/2939 test-other. Runaways are counted over the full set.

| set | condition | WER | B-WER | runaways |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| test-clean | none | 2.23% | 9.45% | 0 |
| test-clean | `hotwords`, N=100 | 2.02% | 5.05% | 3 |
| test-clean | model card English recipe via `prompt`, N=100 | 2.46% | 6.16% | 23 |
| test-clean | `hotwords`, N=1000 | 12.67% | 17.39% | 134 |
| test-other | none | 4.93% | 21.54% | 1 |
| test-other | `hotwords`, N=100 | 3.83% | 10.39% | 1 |
| test-other | model card English recipe via `prompt`, N=100 | 4.45% | 12.43% | 17 |
| test-other | `hotwords`, N=1000 | 14.04% | 27.27% | 151 |

</details>

## Details

- **Root cause**: #39674 added `TranscriptionRequest.hotwords` and `SpeechToTextParams.hotwords`, but each model must map it into its own prompt format; the MOSS implementation (#47729) never read the field.
- **One hint for all languages**: the model card has a Chinese default instruction with `热词提示：` and an English variant with `Hotwords:`. On English audio, the Chinese default with `热词提示：` beat the English recipe on both LibriSpeech sets (B-WER 5.05% vs 6.16% and 10.39% vs 12.43%) and had far fewer runaways (3 vs 23 and 1 vs 17), so there is no per-language switch.
- **The list is passed through verbatim** (stripped) rather than re-joined, matching how Fun-ASR treats the same field.
- **Limitation (model behavior, not this patch)**: long lists (400 zh / 1000 en terms) cause repetition loops or leak list terms after the transcript, and accuracy drops below the no-hotword baseline even after excluding runaways. The docs now advise keeping the list short; callers can bound runaways with `max_completion_tokens`.
- **Eval caveats**: English normalization was lowercasing and punctuation stripping only, with no number normalization, so absolute numbers are not comparable to papers, but conditions are comparable to each other. Runaway filtering favors the N=1000 rows. Greedy decoding only.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to write the patch, tests, and evaluation scripts, and to run the validation above on my machine.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Size the HiSparse hot buffer from the rounded sparse top-k width
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

HiSparse sized its scheduler hot-cache allocation from `index_topk`, while GLM-5.3-Flash allocates a wider, padded top-k buffer. This updates the existing fix in #60805 following review; related GLM support is tracked in #61243 and #60072.

## Claims

- Keep GLM's width calculation in its model definition, shared with MTP. Pass the actual allocated width through `MLAAttentionSpec` so HiSparse does not need to import GPU model code in the scheduler.
- Allow custom `device_buffer_size` values whose physical allocation includes block padding, by removing the startup equality assertion.

## Validation

All applicable pre-commit hooks pass, including Ruff, mypy, test tethering, and forbidden-import checks. No new tests are included; existing MLA test fixtures only gain the metadata field required by the code change.

The normal focused pytest run cannot collect on this macOS ARM checkout due to missing vLLM dependencies. The documented precompiled editable install also fails because no macOS ARM wheel is available. CUDA startup, model evaluation, and full pytest remain to be run in a supported environment.

## Details

For `index_topk=2048` and `index_kpool=4`, the model reserves the incomplete pool tail and rounds the buffer width to 2176. With seven speculative tokens, HiSparse therefore needs `9 * 2176 = 19584` default hot rows per request, rather than `9 * 2048 = 18432`. The scheduler now receives this width from the model's cache specification, preserving the model's own sizing rules.

A user-selected capacity can differ from the physical allocation: 129 logical rows occupy three 64-row blocks. Registration must accept that padding.

AI assistance was used to implement and review these changes. The existing PR is updated rather than opening a duplicate; no broader GLM enablement is included.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][AuxOutput] Do not rescan referenced keys in the routed-experts store
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Split from #62044 (by @faresobeid): only the store eviction fix.

`BlockObjectStore` kept referenced and unreferenced objects in one LRU, and eviction scanned it from the oldest key, skipping referenced ones. Keys referenced by running requests pile up at the front, so every `put()` that had to evict rescanned all of them on the writer thread. #62044 measured about 9 ms per `put` with 300k keys, and reports that removing this rescan cut the writer thread from 281 s to 2.3 s over 20 RL steps on GLM-4.5-Air, for +15.6% throughput.

The store now follows `BlockPool`'s free block queue: the LRU holds only unreferenced objects.

- `_slots` maps every stored key to its slot.
- A key leaves the LRU when its reference count goes from 0 to 1, and goes back to its tail when the count drops to 0. Within one `put()`, released keys end up after the batch's objects, in release order, as before.
- Eviction takes keys from the front of the LRU. As before, it skips keys stored by the same `put()` unless that call also releases them; they are at the tail by then.

With balanced retains and releases, eviction order, victims and errors are the same as before. Releasing a key that is not referenced raises `KeyError`, as before; keys released earlier in that call go to the tail of the LRU instead of keeping their old position, so later victims can differ. The writer thread stops after that error.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/distributed/aux_output_connector/test_store.py
```

`test_store_eviction_does_not_rescan_referenced_keys` fills a store with 900 referenced and 100 unreferenced objects, then makes 100 `put()` calls. The referenced keys are a `str` subclass that counts its own hashes, so any dict or set lookup of a referenced key is counted, whatever container the store uses. The test also checks that the 100 unreferenced objects are the ones evicted and that every referenced object stays readable. It does not touch store internals.

## Test Result

- `test_store.py`: 65 passed.
- The new test counts 0 hashes of referenced keys with this change and 180,000 on `main` (limit 900). It also fails on `main` with `_references` or `_lru` renamed.
- Differential fuzz against `main` (not part of the PR), 5,000 random sequences of `put` (duplicate keys, varying payloads, retains, releases) and `get` on stores of 1 to 10 slots:
  - balanced references: stored keys, allocated keys, reference counts and eviction order are identical after every operation;
  - with unreferenced releases: the store invariant holds after every operation; 404 sequences pick different victims after the `KeyError`.
  - Evicting from the wrong end of the LRU differs on the first sequence.

## Benchmark

GLM-4.5-Air, one GB200 node (TP4), `gpu_memory_utilization=0.9` (2,434,064 KV tokens, 167,341 store objects), `max_model_len=20480`, routed experts enabled. Each step is an RL-style rollout: 64 prompts x 8 samples (512 sequences), 1k-16k output tokens with `ignore_eos`, seeded per step so every run generates exactly the same 13,448,609 tokens over 3 steps. Both arms use the same 2026-10-16 nightly image and differ only in `store.py`; runs are ordered main, PR, PR, main. The store is set to 1.1x the KV-sized default so that `main` does not hit the full-KV crash fixed by #62044. Writer-thread time is the sum of `BlockObjectStore.put` wall time.

| Run | Step 0 | Step 1 | Step 2 | Throughput | Writer `put` time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 510.5 s | 487.8 s | 425.5 s | 9,446 tok/s | 526.0 s |
| PR | 417.2 s | 415.0 s | 414.4 s | 10,788 tok/s | 4.4 s |
| PR | 417.5 s | 415.1 s | 413.9 s | 10,789 tok/s | 7.3 s |
| main | 420.0 s | 545.5 s | 549.4 s | 8,878 tok/s | 617.7 s |

Throughput is +17.7% (9,162 to 10,788 tok/s on average). On `main`, the step time follows the writer-thread time: about 420 s at 140 s of `put`, about 545 s at 240 s. With `gpu_memory_utilization=0.5` (753,552 KV tokens, about 52k objects) the writer was busy for 17% of each step on `main` and throughput was unchanged (5,868 vs 5,897 tok/s), so the gain needs a store large enough for the rescan to delay the engine.

### Reproduce

Run the script below once with `main` and once with this PR, on one node with 4 GPUs (`max_bytes` is 1.1x the default store size for this model and KV size):

```python
import random
import sys
import time

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

WORDS = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta", "prime", "integer", "triangle", "sum",
         "product", "remainder", "circle", "radius", "matrix", "vector", "angle"]


def main():
    model, steps = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
    llm = LLM(
        model=model,
        tensor_parallel_size=4,
        gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,
        max_model_len=20480,
        enable_return_routed_experts=True,
        aux_output_config={"max_bytes": 985_303_808},
        seed=0,
    )
    for step in range(steps):
        rng = random.Random(1000 + step)
        prompts, params = [], []
        for g in range(64):
            body = " ".join(rng.choice(WORDS) for _ in range(rng.randint(150, 900)))
            text = f"Problem {step}-{g}: {body}. Solve it step by step."
            for _ in range(8):
                prompts.append(text)
                params.append(SamplingParams(temperature=1.0, ignore_eos=True,
                                             max_tokens=rng.randint(1024, 16384)))
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        outs = llm.generate(prompts, params, use_tqdm=False)
        dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
        gen = sum(len(c.token_ids) for o in outs for c in o.outputs)
        print(f"step {step}: {dt:.1f} s, {gen} tokens, {gen / dt:.0f} tok/s", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```bash
python repro.py zai-org/GLM-4.5-Air 3
```

A single step with this script gave 459.3 s on `main` and 417.7 s with this PR for the same 4,543,356 tokens.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][KV Offload][P2P] Report NIXL submission failures and escalate persistent faults to session teardown
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

This PR fixes two P2P data-plane failures and adds a reconnect backoff. Each part is its own commit (the backoff plus a follow-up that counts faults in its log, then a commit addressing review), so they can be reviewed, or split, independently:

1. **Submission failures are reported to the fetching peer** (fixes #60204). A NIXL error raised while submitting a fetch's WRITE escaped to the session dispatcher, so the peer waited its full 30 s load timeout before recomputing.
2. **Persistent NIXL faults end the session** (fixes #60205 together with #60279). A peer with a stale NIXL registration but a healthy control plane failed every WRITE for the rest of the process. This also answers @snadampal's review question on this PR about recovering the peer instead of fast-failing forever.
3. **Reconnect backoff.** A peer that faults again right after each re-handshake backs off before the next reconnect, as the NixlConnector does for invalid peers.

#61500 independently traces the same root cause in NIXL 1.5.0 for the NixlConnector's pull path: after one `REMOTE_DISCONNECT`, the UCX endpoint stays `FAILED` until the remote agent is re-added. Its production numbers show the before/after effect.

Replaces #55553 (closed in favour of this, by @Etelis). Together with #60279 it covers #55181.

## Claims

**Commit 1 (transfer scope)**
- An error from `make_prepped_xfer` / `transfer` takes the existing fail-fast path. The round fails, the peer gets `TransferDoneMsg(success=False)`, the store job fails at once, and the created handle is released.
- `transfer()` returning `"ERR"` (how the bindings report a failed post) is a failed submission. Previously it was ignored and the handle parked inflight.
- `on_fetch` no longer finalizes a round a second time after a failed submission. That raised `KeyError` in the store-first and finish-before-fetch orderings.

**Commit 2 (escalation)**
- `NixlTransport` classifies each NIXL failure in one place:
  - `nixlRemoteDisconnectError` / `nixlNotFoundError` fault the peer at once.
  - A `check_xfer_state` that raises faults the peer at once (commit 5). NIXL's binding raises for every error status (only `SUCCESS` / `IN_PROG` are returned), so a raise is how a failed WRITE is reported, e.g. `nixlBackendError` for a UCX error.
  - Any other failure (a failed submission, or a transfer in state `"ERR"`) is a strike, and 3 consecutive strikes with no success between them fault the peer. Strikes from one `poll()` batch are applied after the batch is classified, so a `DONE` for the peer anywhere in it counts as the success between (commit 5).
  - Only `nixlRemoteDisconnectError` ends a transfer whose state check raised. Any other raise keeps it inflight, because its WRITE may still be landing (#59790 measured bytes landing while the handle raised `nixlNotFoundError`); the peer fault and the drain cap below bound it.
  - The fault is reported through a new `PollResult.peer_fault`.
- After a fault, no new WRITE goes to that peer. Once its inflight WRITEs drain (capped at 10 s), the session sends `DisconnectMsg`. The existing reap then tears down both sides, and the next request re-registers them.
- Every session death records a reason, and the manager's `peer X down (<reason>)` log reports it. Examples: `data plane: NIXL_ERR_REMOTE_DISCONNECT`, `protocol error: …`, `handshake timed out`, `lookup response timed out`, `control connection lost`.

**Commits 3–4 (reconnect backoff)**
- After reaping a session that ended on a data-plane fault, the faulting side records a per-peer backoff. The first fault reconnects at once. A repeat fault within 60 s of the previous wait expiring doubles the wait, from 1 s up to 60 s, as in the NixlConnector (#55471, #61500). Expiry is by time alone: no successful transfer is required, so a peer that is only idle for 60 s starts over at an immediate reconnect. Control-plane deaths don't back off.
- During the wait, outbound connects to the peer are skipped, so lookups fall back to local prefill. An inbound connect from the peer gets `DisconnectMsg` and is closed, so the peer falls back at once instead of waiting for its handshake deadline. There is no protocol change.
- The peer-down log carries a per-peer lifetime count of data-plane faults, e.g. `peer X down (data plane: …); data-plane fault #7; reconnect backoff 8s`. Unlike the backoff it never expires, so a peer that keeps faulting under traffic too sparse to escalate shows up as a rising count rather than as a series of unrelated faults.

## Validation

```
pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/ -q    # 308 passed (commit 1 alone: 281)
pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/ -q        # 554 passed, 12 skipped
pre-commit run --files <changed files>        # passed, incl. mypy
```

| Scenario | Before | After | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `transfer` / `make_prepped_xfer` raises, including when the release also fails | escapes to the dispatcher; no `TransferDoneMsg`; round stays alive | `None`, handle released, no inflight leak | `test_write_blocks_submission_exception_returns_failure` |
| `transfer()` returns `"ERR"` | handle parked inflight | `None`, handle released | `test_write_blocks_transfer_err_status_returns_failure` |
| Failed submit, store-first or finish-before-fetch | `KeyError` from double finalize | one finalize, one `TransferDoneMsg(False)` | `test_write_blocks_failure_finalizes_with_failure[*]`; fails without the `on_fetch` change |
| 3 failed WRITEs to a peer whose control plane is healthy (#60205) | every later WRITE fails, session never ends | peer faulted → drain → `DisconnectMsg` → reap | `TestNixlPeerFaults`, `TestPeerFaultEscalation` |
| `check_xfer_state` raises (`nixlBackendError`) while other WRITEs to the peer succeed | one strike, reset by the successes; transfer stays inflight for good: ~40 s consumer stall, pins and session held | peer faulted at once; transfer kept until it drains or the 10 s drain cap, then reaped | `test_raising_state_check_faults_the_peer_and_keeps_the_transfer`, `test_raise_faults_despite_a_success_in_the_batch` |
| `check_xfer_state` raises `nixlNotFoundError` | peer faulted; transfer kept, warning on every poll | peer faulted; transfer kept (not terminal, per #59790); warns once | `test_not_found_state_check_keeps_the_transfer`, `test_not_found_in_cancel_keeps_the_transfer`, `test_raising_state_check_warns_once` |
| strikes=2, one poll batch with `ERR` iterated before 3 `DONE`s | peer faulted, session torn down | strikes reset, no fault | `test_success_in_the_same_batch_prevents_the_fault`; fails on the previous code |
| Fault while WRITEs are inflight | — | new rounds fail fast; disconnect only after the drain or the 10 s cap | `test_fault_waits_for_inflight_then_disconnects`, `test_fault_disconnects_after_drain_deadline` |
| Peer faults again right after each re-handshake | reconnect, register and fail on every request | waits 0, 1, 2, 4 … 60 s; outbound skipped, inbound told to disconnect; resets 60 s after the last wait expires; the logged fault count keeps growing across the reset | `TestReconnectBackoff` |

**End to end on real NIXL** (two H200 pods, PDConnector + P2P tier, Llama-3.2-1B, NIXL 1.5.0, commit dc2d0b94fc). Happy path in both proxy modes: correct output and a 95–96 % external prefix-cache hit rate (240 of 254 prompt tokens pulled per request). A persistent fault was then forced with a test-only hook (not in this PR) that makes the prefiller's `transfer()` return `"ERR"` while a flag file exists:
- Every fetch failed fast: 20 consecutive requests finished in 1.6–2.3 s with correct output (recomputed locally), with no 30 s load timeout.
- Each 3 strikes ended the session: prefiller `peer D down (data plane: 3 consecutive transfer failures …); data-plane fault #1 … #6`, decoder `peer P down (peer disconnected)`; both sides re-registered on the next request.
- The backoff grew 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s; during the 8 s and 16 s waits the prefiller logged `rejecting inbound peer … (2.5s / 10.6s left)` and the decoder fell back at once.
- After the flag was cleared, hits returned (240/254) on the fresh session, with no crash, `KeyError` or segfault on either side.

**State-check faults, end to end** (same setup, commit a1cc819cb6). A second test-only hook makes the prefiller's `check_xfer_state` raise an exception named after the real binding class while a flag file exists. That is how NIXL 1.5.0 reports a failed WRITE: the binding raises for every error status.

| Injected fault | Faulted request | Prefiller log | After clearing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| every check raises `nixlBackendError` | 11.7–11.9 s, correct output (recomputed) | peer faulted on the first raise; `disconnecting once inflight transfers drain`; `peer D down (data plane: check_xfer_state raised nixlBackendError …)` exactly 10 s later; backoff 0, 1, 2 s over three faults | 240/254 hits |
| every check raises `nixlNotFoundError` | 11.6–11.8 s, correct output | peer faulted (`NIXL_ERR_NOT_FOUND`); the transfer stays inflight (not terminal, per #59790) until the 10 s drain cap, then teardown | 256/256 hits |
| one transfer keeps raising while all others succeed | 12.2 s for that request; the next two 1.8 s with 240/254 hits | one fault, teardown at the 10 s cap, reconnect 6 s later | 256/256 hits |

- The last row is the case the previous revision left unbounded: its single strike was reset by the other successes, so the transfer stayed inflight for good, holding its pins and session. It is now torn down within the 10 s drain cap. Each faulted request costs the cap plus normal latency, versus an expected ~40 s (load timeout plus abort-ack timeout) before; that before-number was not measured.
- One `check_xfer_state failed` warning per transfer, not one per poll.
- One EngineCore per pod throughout; no crash, `KeyError` or segfault. Happy path afterwards in PD mode with the hook removed: 95.9 % hit rate.

These exercise faults that leave both processes alive. A genuinely restarted peer still can't be tested here: restarting either P2P peer segfaults the survivor in NIXL `loadRemoteMD`, a pre-existing problem (see #60205).

## Details

**Root cause (commit 1).** `_submit_transfer` fails fast only when `write_blocks` *returns* `None`. `NixlTransport.write_blocks` caught nothing, so a NIXL error reached `P2PSession._on_message`, which only logs. The dispatcher's disconnect-after-5-errors guard doesn't fire either, because successful messages in between reset its counter.

**Root cause (commit 2).** Only control-plane signals can mark a peer dead: heartbeat, protocol error, handshake, registration, and lookup timeout (#56836). Data-plane failures were never an input. In #60205 the heartbeats and lookups stay healthy while NIXL's endpoints for the peer are stale.

**Flow after a persistent fault (prefiller P writes into decoder D):**
1. D sends `FetchMsg`. P's `write_blocks` fails, or `check_xfer_state` raises in `poll`. The round fails with `TransferDone(False)` and D recomputes.
2. After 3 strikes, or one decisive error, P's `poll(D)` returns `peer_fault`. P's server role stops submitting, so later fetches from D fail fast.
3. Once P's inflight WRITEs to D drain, P sends `DisconnectMsg` and marks the connection dead with reason `data plane: …`.
4. P's manager reaps the session: it fails its jobs and calls `remove_remote_peer(D)`. D receives `DisconnectMsg` and runs the same reap for P.
5. D's next request opens a new connection, `ConnectMsg` goes both ways, and both sides register fresh. The registration generation keeps a late async registration from reviving the old peer.

**Design choice: one death path.** A data-plane fault ends a peer the same way a control-plane fault does. The transport never re-registers a peer in place. The alternative was `remove_remote_peer` after N failures, inside the transport. That tears down only one side: the session still believes the peer is registered, and the peer keeps *our* stale registration. It also cannot work for a restarted peer. Reusing the reap means no new teardown code.

**Tradeoffs and limitations.**
- A `check_xfer_state` that raises with anything but `REMOTE_DISCONNECT` stays inflight, as #59790 established: it isn't provably terminal, and its WRITE may still be landing. It faults the peer at once, so the session's 10 s drain cap bounds how long it can last. The cost is that one failed state check tears down a peer that is otherwise working (a re-handshake, plus the backoff if it repeats). Treating `nixlBackendError` / `nixlCancelledError` as terminal (the UCX request finished with an error) would avoid the drain wait, but needs evidence that NIXL's UCX backend reports a handle's error only once all of its requests are done; left for a follow-up.
- The disconnect waits for inflight WRITEs because D frees their destination blocks on `DisconnectMsg`. The 10 s cap trades that guarantee for not hanging on a stuck transfer, the same exposure a heartbeat death has today.
- The thresholds (3 strikes, 10 s drain, 1→60 s backoff) are conservative constants, not measured values. The backoff uses the NixlConnector's numbers.
- The backoff forgets a peer by time, not by a successful transfer, matching the NixlConnector. Under sparse traffic a persistently broken peer therefore cycles at a 0 s backoff (3 fast-failing requests that recompute locally, plus one re-registration per cycle); the fault count in the log makes that visible. Requiring a success before forgetting would close the gap but needs a transport→manager success signal, and is better done for both connectors together.
- Only the faulting side knows about the backoff. During the wait, the other peer still tries to connect on each new request and is turned away within one round trip; concurrent requests share the pending attempt. A retry-after hint in `DisconnectMsg` would remove that, at the cost of a protocol change.

**Relation to other PRs.**
- #59790 (merged) provides the sibling drain before `TransferDone(False)`; this PR builds on it.
- #60279 (narrowed to `remove_remote_peer` teardown robustness) is complementary. Expect a one-line conflict in `remove_remote_peer` for whichever lands second.
- #61500 (NixlConnector, pull mode) releases a peer after a failed read, with the same backoff. It touches no shared code. That connector's teardown is one-sided because only the decoder holds the remote registration; P2P registers both ways, so here both sides tear down.
- #49632 marks any `check_xfer_state` raise as failed and releases the handle, which can free a handle whose WRITE is still landing. Here such a transfer stays inflight and is bounded by the escalation instead.

**Changes since the previous revision.**
- Rebased onto main, which now includes #59790, #56836 and #58168.
- Dropped the `try/except` around `write_blocks` in `_submit_transfer`, and its test. The contract, now documented in `data/base.py`, is that transports don't raise for NIXL errors.
- Added commits 2–5. Commit 4 adds the per-peer fault count to the peer-down log and corrects the description of when the backoff resets (time since the last wait expired, not time healthy); behaviour is unchanged. Commit 5 addresses review of `poll()`: strikes per batch, and any raising state check faults the peer (`NOT_FOUND` is deliberately not terminal; see the review thread).
- About 330 source lines are added, comments and docstrings included: roughly 30 in commit 1, 190 in commit 2, 60 in commit 3, 20 in commit 4 and 30 in commit 5. Each commit stands alone, so the PR can be split along those lines if reviewers prefer.

commits.pr_title: [Doc][ROCm] Align Kimi-K3 MI355X recipe with InferenceX #4215
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Align the Kimi-K3 MI355X TP8 recipe and its AgentX guide with [SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX#4215](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4215) (branch revision `6e72cbc11234e624d66b8fc5eaddac50068db15c`), which supersedes the InferenceX #3833 lane that vllm-project/recipes#1093 documented. Recipes for vLLM-served models now live here (#61302), so this changes only `recipes/models/moonshotai/Kimi-K3.yaml`.

## Claims

- MI355X TP8 command builder: drop the `--load-format fastsafetensors` override so the AMD profile's default loader applies (on the lane's image, fastsafetensors ran out of GPU memory while loading weights, [InferenceX run 38975751686](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38975751686)), and add `AITER_FLYDSL_STAGE2_FP8=1`.
- AgentX guide: the ten #4215 cells (dcp1 c1/c4; dcp8 c4-c60 with SimpleCPUOffload), per-cell online FP8 target quantization (c1 no longer ignores `*in_proj_qkvgfab`; every other cell quantizes only `in_proj_qkvgfab`), `VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4` with `VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_MIN_SIZE_BYTES_MB=16`, the pinned image, and the golden-AL table for 7/5/4 draft tokens.
- Fix two errors in the previous guide: `seq -s, 2 "$MAX_CAPTURE"` captured odd CUDA-graph sizes (now even only, as the text states), and `AITER_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION` is not read by vLLM (the lane sets `VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION`).
- Real serving stays on block verification; synthetic acceptance stays in the separate throughput-only section. The `Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark` draft stays at its shipped precision: BF16 weights and activations, FP8 KV.

## Validation

- Ground truth: the #4215 lane recipe and `amd-master.yaml` entry at `6e72cbc` are identical to in-PR commit `8a2aec3`, which passed all ten cells and their evals in [InferenceX run 39002920671](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/39002920671) on `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-rocm100-49cb2bbf71cfd36ee5aa33d1e184b1cddff55294`, with real block verification: GSM8K 0.969 strict/flexible (dcp8 c60) and `kimi_tool_call_schema_full` 0.978-0.998 (nine cells).
- From vllm-project/recipes main (`b8bec4f`), pointed at this checkout: `node scripts/validate-source.mjs --source vllm --dir <vllm>/recipes` (valid, 215 recipes), `node scripts/build-recipes-api.mjs` and `pnpm build` all pass; the rendered MI355X builder command and guide section were checked in a local browser.
- Generated-command diff against this branch's base: of the 71 Kimi-K3 JSON API files, only `hw/mi355x.json`, the two MI355X Mooncake KV-store strategies (which reuse the TP8 command) and `Kimi-K3.json` (guide, `date_updated`) change. The MI355X command changes only `--load-format fastsafetensors` to `auto` and adds `AITER_FLYDSL_STAGE2_FP8=1`; every other hardware and strategy file is identical.
- The guide's reproduction script, run for each of the ten cells with `vllm` stubbed, resolves arguments and environment equal to the #4215 lane: draft tokens, `--max-num-seqs`, `--max-num-batched-tokens`, even capture sizes 2..max, quantization, speculative and offload configs, DCP8, QuickReduce and `PYTHONHASHSEED`. Stale #3833 cells (dcp8 c1/c2/c12/c14/c44) are rejected. All 12 guide bash blocks pass `bash -n`, and all 12 embedded JSON values parse.
- `pre-commit run --files recipes/models/moonshotai/Kimi-K3.yaml` passes; `git diff --check` is clean.
- No new GPU run: the recipe documents the exact configuration validated by the InferenceX run above.

## Details

- Not duplicate work: no open PR in vllm-project/vllm or vllm-project/recipes references InferenceX #4215, `in_proj_qkvgfab`, `AITER_FLYDSL_STAGE2_FP8` or `VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_MIN_SIZE_BYTES_MB` (searched 2026-10-18); the open Kimi-K3 MI355X PRs here are kernel changes.
- INT4 QuickReduce is lossy, so as before it stays out of the builder and appears only in the exact reproduction command. The 16 MiB floor keeps it off the draft: the draft's all-reduces carry at most 600 draft-step tokens x 7,168 BF16 values (about 8.2 MiB at c60), and its context projection is replicated.
- `AITER_FLYDSL_STAGE2_FP8=1` stores the FlyDSL MoE down-projection route outputs as MXFP8 before the top-k sum. It changes only the target's MoE (the DSpark draft MLP is dense) and the lane sets it at every cell, so it goes in the builder. `AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND=0` is not read on the SiTUv2 path and stays out of both, as before.
- Per-cell settings (`--max-num-seqs`, batched tokens, graph sizes, target quantization) remain guide-only; the builder keeps its general defaults.
- Not changed: the MI355X disaggregated P/D example still uses `fastsafetensors` and the rolling `nightly` image; it is a separate deployment that #4215 does not cover.
- AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5 in Cursor) was used to prepare this change and its validation.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Weight Cache] Include RoPE parameters in IPC cache key
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Prevent IPC weight cache reuse across different text RoPE configurations, which could otherwise cause engines to use incompatible cached rotary buffers.

## Claims

- Reject incompatible RoPE configurations through the existing cache-key mismatch and disk fallback handling.
- Preserve cache reuse for matching configurations, including explicitly specified defaults.
- Preserve standalone in-place weight reloading when model construction normalizes RoPE parameters.

## Validation

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_weight_cache.py \
  -k 'not cold_start_and_warm_restart' -q
```

18 passed, 3 deselected. Tests cover RoPE configuration differences, explicit defaults, nested multimodal text configs, and startup versus reload matching.

Separately validated with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on an H800 (TP=1, V1 runner, eager mode):

- Matching configurations load through IPC and match normal disk loading.
- Different theta values raise a configuration mismatch when fallback is disabled.
- With fallback enabled, both `zero_copy` and `copy` modes match normal loading with the requested configuration in generated token IDs and prompt logprobs.

A CPU regression check using the DeepseekV2 attention constructor and IPC protocol verified that standalone `load_weights` accepts constructor-normalized RoPE parameters and rejects mismatched theta values.

All applicable pre-commit checks passed. The three existing model E2E tests were not run. GPU validation covers startup, not in-place reloading.

## Details

The daemon exports non-persistent buffers, including rotary caches, but `WeightCacheKey` previously omitted RoPE parameters. Engines using the same checkpoint with different RoPE settings could therefore reuse incompatible buffers.

Add a fingerprint of `hf_text_config.rope_parameters` to the cache key. For standalone in-place reloading, also accept the daemon's post-construction RoPE fingerprint, since model constructors can normalize these parameters. Startup still requires the original fingerprint, and all other cache-key checks remain unchanged.

Test ran successfully on my local machine.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Core] Keep the EAGLE-reachable SWA tail at a shared-prefix junction
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

This PR fixes cross-request prefix reuse for sliding-window groups under EAGLE/MTP with sparse prefix-cache retention. The shared-prefix junction pin from #47782 kept a sliding-window tail one block too high, so requests that share only a prefix got no prefix-cache hit at all. The fix also pins the tail one block lower, which is where an EAGLE sibling's hit actually lands.

## Claims

- Under sparse retention, a sibling request that shares only a prefix now gets a prefix-cache hit when the drafter's groups are sliding-window and the full-attention groups are not EAGLE groups. On Step-5-Preview with MTP, the GSM8K 5-shot prefix goes from 0 hit tokens to a hit on every request after the first two.
- Nothing changes without EAGLE, or when every group is flagged as an EAGLE group. In those cases the junction already sits one block lower, because the full-attention group drops its block too.
- The cost is one extra cached block per sliding-window group for each request that registers a junction.

## Validation

**Unit test.** `test_swa_shared_prefix_reuse_under_zero_retention` gets a `use_eagle` case that flags only the SWA group, as https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61455 does for drafters. It fails on main (0 instead of 48 hit tokens) and passes with the fix.

```
pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py tests/v1/core/test_single_type_kv_cache_manager.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py tests/v1/core/prefix_cache \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_coordinator.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_scheduler.py
620 passed, 2 errors
```

The 2 errors are `test_hybrid_prefix_cache_hit_rate`, which needs a GPU and a model checkpoint (the run was CPU-only). On a wider set (`tests/v1/core`, Mooncake Store and offloading connector unit tests), the failure set with and without this PR is identical (GPU- or model-dependent tests), apart from the new case.

**End to end.** Step-5-Preview (MTP layers are sliding-window, the target also has full-attention DSA layers), 4x GB300, TP4 + EP, MTP k=3. Prefix caching runs with `--prefix-cache-retention-interval 1024`. The test runs on the Step5 preview branch of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61727, with this change applied.

12 GSM8K 5-shot prompts are sent one at a time. They share a 565-token prefix, and every prompt is shorter than 1024 tokens.

| | request 1 | request 2 | requests 3–12 |
|---|---|---|---|
| no MTP | 0 | 0 | 560 each |
| MTP k=3, without this PR | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| MTP k=3, this PR | 0 | 0 | 544 each |

Request 2 detects the junction, so later requests can hit. 544 is one block below the 560-token junction, which is the deepest hit an EAGLE lookup can verify.

Full GSM8K (1319 questions, concurrency 64, MTP k=3, Mooncake Store connector on):

| | without this PR | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| local prefix-cache hit tokens / queried | 0 / 839,793 | 737,520 / 839,793 (87.8%) |
| accuracy | 0.933 | 0.935 |
| Mooncake Store replay vs GPU-cache replay | 64/64 bit-identical | 64/64 bit-identical |

## Details

**Root cause.**
1. Request A runs alone.
2. Request B shares a prefix with A, but under sparse retention only A's full-attention blocks are still cached. `get_computed_blocks` reports the junction J as the full-attention hit length (B's shared prefix floored to a block), and B pins J.
3. The sliding-window mask keeps the `need`-block tail at J. Under EAGLE, that tail is shifted one block right, to include the block past J as the lookahead (#44082). This is right for a replay of the same prompt.
4. The block past J holds B's own tokens, so for request C it is not shared. C's SWA lookup must verify one block past its hit, so its best hit is J − block_size. That hit needs the window one block lower than the pinned tail, and the lowest block was never kept.
5. C gets no hit and pins the same J again, so no later request ever hits.

When every group takes the EAGLE drop (no group flagged), the full-attention hit is already one block lower, so J lands where the SWA hit can verify. The bug therefore shows only when a sliding-window group is an EAGLE group and the full-attention group that reports the junction is not. Step5 MTP already met this under the older "group holding the last registered layer" rule. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61455 makes per-group flags the general rule: drafters whose layers are sliding-window now flag only those groups.

**Fix.** Under EAGLE, `cache_blocks` registers both J and J − block_size as reachable boundaries. The masks overlap, so this keeps one extra block. Replay boundaries are unchanged, because they already account for the EAGLE drop (#54713, #61012). Mamba checkpointing reads `shared_prefix_boundary` directly and is unaffected.

**Not covered.** `OffloadingConnector` builds its own reachable boundaries from `shared_prefix_boundary` and is not changed here.

---

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][DSv4] Require explicit MXFP4 opt-in for MegaMoE shared-expert fusion
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Follow-up to #61004. Fusing DeepSeek-V4's shared expert into AITER MegaMoE requantizes it from FP8 to MXFP4. With this PR, that requires an explicit opt-in through the online quantization API instead of a dedicated env var, and it goes through the shared fused-shared-expert (FSE) helpers.

## Claims

- Removes `VLLM_ROCM_AITER_MEGA_MOE_FUSE_SHARED_EXPERTS`. Under `--moe-backend aiter_mega_moe`, the existing `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS` requests the fusion.
- The shared expert is fused only when it is explicitly requantized to MXFP4:
  ```bash
  VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1 vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro --moe-backend aiter_mega_moe ... \
      --quantization-config.targets '{"*shared_experts*": "mxfp4"}'
  ```
  Without that target, a warning is logged and the shared expert stays unfused in checkpoint precision (FP8).
- No model-specific logic:
  - The decision goes through `resolve_layer_fused_shared_expert` / `is_shared_expert_quant_fse_compatible`, which now take a `moe_backend` argument.
  - The requantization reuses `get_and_maybe_dequant_weights` and the `ONLINE_SHARED_EXPERT_QUANTIZERS` from #55686.
- Kernel, routing and performance are unchanged from #61004.

## Validation

DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MI355X, DEP4, `--moe-backend aiter_mega_moe`. GSM8K: lm-eval, 5-shot.

| `--quantization-config.targets` | Shared expert | GSM8K (strict) |
|---|---|--:|
| `{"*shared_experts*": "mxfp4"}` | fused, MXFP4 | 0.9469 ± 0.006 |
| none | unfused, FP8 + warning | 0.9545 ± 0.006 |

```
INFO  Quantizing 122 layers of types: ffn.shared_experts.down_proj: 61 (from targets: *shared_experts*, mxfp4); ffn.shared_experts.gate_up_proj: 61 (...)
WARNING  VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS is enabled but cannot be enabled - skipping for this layer: AITER MegaMoE fuses the shared experts only when --quantization-config.targets requantizes them to MXFP4.
```

Unit tests:
- `tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_aiter_mega_moe.py` covers `is_shared_expert_quant_fse_compatible` with the MegaMoE backend.
- `tests/model_executor/layers/test_fused_shared_expert.py::test_online_mxfp4_shared_expert_rejects_quark_weight_only_mxfp4_fse` keeps Quark weight-only routed experts incompatible with an `mxfp4` shared-expert target.

## Details

- **Activation key.** MegaMoE (a8w4) quantizes every slot's activations to MXFP8 itself. A `"mxfp4"` target cannot express "MXFP4 weights, MXFP8 activations", so for MegaMoE only the weight key is compared. Other backends still compare both keys: Quark weight-only routed experts have no activation key (BF16 activations), which an `mxfp4` target does not match.
- **Why the shared expert is not built with `Mxfp4OnlineLinearMethod`:**
  - `Fp8LinearMethod` has no `dequantize_weight`, so it can't serve as the source for requantization.
  - `AiterMxfp4LinearKernel` pre-shuffles the weights into a layout MegaMoEV2 can't use.

  Instead, the fused shared expert keeps the checkpoint quant config, minus online quantization. MegaMoE then dequantizes it with `get_and_maybe_dequant_weights` and quantizes it with the registered quantizer.
- **Config class.** On CUDA and ROCm, `deepseek_v4_fp8` resolves to the v4.1 `DeepseekV4FP8Config`, so the check accepts both the v4 and v4.1 classes.
- **Breaking:** `VLLM_ROCM_AITER_MEGA_MOE_FUSE_SHARED_EXPERTS`, added in #61004 and present in v0.32.0rc0–rc2, is removed without a deprecation period. Setting it afterwards triggers vLLM's "Unknown vLLM environment variable" warning (an error with `--fail-on-environ-validation`), and the shared expert stays unfused in FP8. If preferred, I can keep it as a deprecated no-op with a warning for one release instead.
- **Out of scope:** making MegaMoE a generic MoE backend in the oracle.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Preserve scheduling priority for online and offline beam search
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Preserve scheduling priority for beam search on `/v1/completions` and `/v1/chat/completions`, and add priority support to offline `LLM.beam_search()`.

## Claims

- Forward the effective body/header priority to every beam expansion instead of silently falling back to engine priority `0`.
- Support offline scalar or per-prompt priorities through the existing priority normalization helper, retaining each prompt's priority across all beam expansions and concurrency batches.
- Preserve default priority `0`, the existing `X-vLLM-Priority` header precedence (including header `0`), and positional-call compatibility.

## Validation

CPU validation with the existing cached GPT2 tokenizer and deterministic mock engines; no GPU inference, real scheduler-dispatch benchmark, or model-quality evaluation. This change forwards scheduling metadata only; model execution, scoring and beam selection are unchanged. The HTTP reproducer checks request-to-engine propagation and frontend response parity, not real inference.

| Coverage | Baseline with regression | Fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Online beam-search suite | 2 failed / 28 passed | 30 passed |
| Completion/chat serving regressions | 4 failed / 2 passed | 6 passed |
| Beam search + offline helpers (offline extension) | 17 failed / 51 passed | 68 passed |
| Combined online/offline + neighboring serving tests | — | 129 passed |
| FastAPI TestClient ASGI reproducer, 16 cases per variant | 4 wrong-priority cases | 16/16 correct |

Offline extension in `55b256be2fb96e08a920132a9a86c3e1ccd0c050` (following the request to cover both modes in this PR): tests exercise real Python beam expansion, request submission and the engine loop with a deterministic fake engine. Cases cover omitted/None/scalar/list/tuple priorities, concurrency batches, an earlier prompt terminating, structured-output active-beam filtering (simulated selector), and mismatched priority lengths. This is request-propagation validation, not native inference or grammar-backend validation.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/samplers/test_beam_search_online.py \
  tests/entrypoints/unit_tests/test_offline_utils.py -q --disable-warnings
```

This command returned **17 failed / 51 passed** with the new tests on the previous production code, then **68 passed** with the offline extension. The combined neighboring command below was extended with `tests/entrypoints/unit_tests/test_offline_utils.py`: **129 passed**, exit 0. Patch-scoped pre-commit checks on the three newly changed files also passed, including mypy and CI test tethering. The submitter confirmed reviewing and running the offline extension before publication.

Both HTTP variants returned 200 throughout, and parsed response JSON matched after excluding only creation timestamps. The reproducer uses real frontend constructors, routing and tokenization but a deterministic mock engine.

Reproduction commands (Linux CPU test environment with test dependencies and cached GPT2 tokenizer):

```bash
export VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 PYTHONPATH="$PWD"

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/samplers/test_beam_search_online.py -q --disable-warnings

.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/completion/test_completion_error.py::test_beam_search_preserves_request_priority \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_beam_search_preserves_request_priority \
  -q --disable-warnings

.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/samplers/test_beam_search_online.py \
  tests/entrypoints/unit_tests/test_offline_utils.py \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/completion/test_completion_error.py \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_beam_search_preserves_request_priority \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_serving_chat_returns_correct_model_name \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_serving_chat_should_set_correct_max_tokens \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_serving_chat_did_set_correct_cache_salt \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_serving_chat_data_parallel_rank_extraction \
  -q --disable-warnings
```

Before the offline extension, after rebasing onto `689effee6d07bfeb0afe42d44046141657238c23` (including #62072), the last command was re-run: **103 passed**, exit 0, including the upstream generation-config EOS regressions and this PR's priority regressions. Patch-scoped `pre-commit run --files` on all six changed files also passed, including mypy and Buildkite test-tethering checks (exit 0). Baseline failures above were observed before the production fix with the same regression tests.

Original RED/GREEN and HTTP validation base: `0c5dd18e7a0ace18d99438fb16b8375572ea76b5`. Rebased onto `689effee6d07bfeb0afe42d44046141657238c23` on October 19; resolved the test insertion conflict by retaining both the upstream EOS tests and this PR's priority tests. Rebased online-only head: `b1dcf9c001cadec2bd2b55095c0aec56bba19d7c`; offline follow-up head: `55b256be2fb96e08a920132a9a86c3e1ccd0c050`. The 103-test suite and six-file pre-commit checks were re-run on this head. The earlier standalone and HTTP results in the table describe the original validation, not a new HTTP run after rebasing. Human review/test completion was confirmed before initial publication; AI assistance was used.

## Details

The ordinary sampling branches already resolve request priority with `_get_priority`. The beam branches skipped that helper, and `BeamSearchOnlineMixin.beam_search` did not accept a priority argument, so every expansion used `engine_client.generate`'s default. Add a defaulted argument at the end of the existing signature and forward it from both serving endpoints through every expansion. No scheduler or model-runner changes. Offline `LLM.beam_search()` gains an optional trailing `priority: int | Sequence[int] | None = None` argument. It reuses `_priority_to_seq`, stores priority on the prompt instance, expands it to current beams and selects it with the same `active_indices` as structured-output filtering before submitting engine requests.

The regressions exercise missing headers, a nonzero header override, an explicit zero header override, omitted/default mixin priority and nonzero mixin priorities. They consume complete frontend responses and check all expansion requests rather than only the initial call.

Duplicate checks refreshed immediately before submission on October 18: open-PR searches for `beam priority` (only unrelated compressed-tensors kernel PR #55232; files inspected), `beam_search priority`, and `57243 in:body` found no same-fix PR. Open beam-title results were also checked against the overnight overlap audit: #60550 handles failed-beam cleanup, #62072 EOS tokens, #52621 stop strings, #59506 length penalty, #60787 encoder reuse, and #36285 structured output. These may touch nearby code but do not address priority propagation. #57243 prompted the adjacent priority-propagation audit; this PR does not claim it introduced the online omission.
